concept_summary: Chronoforge Dawn is an overhead action-RPG set on a post-collapse Earth where neon city-states sit beside alien-terraformed ruins, and it is a ground-up AAA remake of the Chronoforge prototype — same three heroes (Kaida, Vex, Rune), same world, same ATB combat, same settlement economy, rebuilt from a flat Canvas-2D tile grid into a real 3D world rendered under a fixed overhead camera. The player walks a party of three across terrain with genuine elevation and a moving sun, enters cities and buildings to trade and take quests, collides with roaming enemies to drop into staged cinematic ATB battles, and grows a home settlement through four tech tiers. The player wins by reuniting the fractured city-states, reaching the Transcendent tier, and defeating the Void Architect; they lose if the party is wiped or the home base is razed with no reclaim resources left. Dawn is the signature hour — long shadows, warm rim light, cold shadow — and that framing is the bar every scene is judged against.
scope_constraints: IN — Three.js under a fixed overhead camera is the renderer. The world is real 3D geometry with elevation, a moving sun, soft shadows, depth-of-field falloff and weather; characters are rendered through a pixel-snap and palette-quantise pass so they read as sprites.

IN — Every character is a low-poly 3D rig built in code and posed by an animation system, with weapons, armor and accessories as separate meshes attached to named sockets. This is the fix for the prototype's art failure: an image-generation pipeline cannot draw the same hero twice in a new stance or holding a different weapon, and each hero needs roughly forty poses across overworld, battle, portrait and cutscene.
OUT — No sprite-generation pipeline, no binary art assets, no network fetches. Every mesh, texture, VFX and sound is generated in code from noise, SDFs and in-code baking. No PNGs in the repo.
OUT — No Math.random(). Seeded RNG streams only, so every capture and every headless probe run is reproducible.

IN — A verification harness in tools/ ships before the game and gates every claim: deterministic GPU screenshots at named camera presets and times of day, contact sheets, blind A/B pairs, a frame histogram probe, a real-keyboard traversal probe, a door probe that enters and exits every door, a seeded headless battle probe, a battle-camera framing probe, a fog-continuity probe, an economy simulator, a save round-trip differ, a generated-asset digest, and a content census. No agent may claim anything it has not screenshotted or measured.

IN — Every module ships a showcase mode staging a representative scene of just that module, and the page exposes a window.__DAWN__ debug API with post, probe, stats, seek, step, setShot, setTime, battle and teleport.

IN — Build order is strictly stack-ranked and each tier ships playable and verified before the next starts: (1) world and light, (2) traversal, (3) places and interiors, (4) encounters and battle, (5) progression and menus, (6) settlement economy.

IN — Eight named prototype defects must be fixed and each is checkable in a screenshot: square hard-edged fog of war, the visible tile grid, missing shadows and ground contact, the placeless gradient battle background, the flat single-elevation world, grey ghost enemies under fog, 1px neon menu chrome, and the unstyled debug-readout HUD.

IN — The prototype's game design is an input, not a subject for redesign: ATB math, enemy tiers, tech tables, drop tables, economy curves, menu tab structure and keyboard model port forward. The remake replaces presentation, not mechanics.
IN — Performance budget is a hard gate, not a trade-off: 60 fps at 1080p, 16.6 ms frame, no more than 900 draw calls. Disabling a post pass to make one module look better is a defect.
IN — One folder per subsystem with a file-ownership table in CONTRACT.md; no agent edits outside its lane, and all shared-core changes go through a single integrator.

IN — Critics score 0-10 against the prototype itself as the reference: matched shots from games/chronoforge are the 5, the fixed defect list is the 8.5, and pass is 8.5 or above with zero console errors and a green probe. Final gate is a blind A/B where judges see Dawn and the prototype at matched location, time and framing with the order shuffled.
IN — Save/load via browser localStorage, single slot, round-tripping the full game state byte-identical.
IN — Deployable to GitHub Pages as a static build.
OUT — No multiplayer, PvP, or networked play of any kind.
OUT — No procedural map, dungeon, or quest generation. The world is handcrafted.
OUT — No voice acting, animated cutscenes, or CG cinematics. Scripted sprite choreography and portrait-flash text frames only.
OUT — No mobile or touch input for v1. Desktop mouse and keyboard only.
OUT — No real-time strategy combat. All combat is turn-based ATB, and base raids are scripted story beats rather than live attacks.

IN — Inventory ports the prototype interaction model verbatim: an owned-item grid plus three equipped slots per hero (weapon/armor/accessory), swappable BOTH by click-item-then-click-slot and by drag-and-drop, with a stat-diff preview showing the plus/minus on every affected stat BEFORE the swap commits. Equipping validates the slot and returns the displaced item to the grid. The 20 entries in the prototype ITEM_DEFS and every enemy drop table port forward unchanged.

IN — duel.mjs reports the loot distribution across its seeded battles, not just combat resolution: observed drop rate per item against the declared table, and any item that never dropped. A build where loot silently never fires must fail the gate rather than pass it.

IN — The exploration camera is fixed: 55-degree pitch, no player rotation, no player zoom, trailing the party with damping. This is an art-direction decision — a single known framing means every vista can be hand-tuned and no unlit or unfinished angle is ever reachable.

IN — Battle happens in place with no scene swap and no load. The camera swings laterally and pushes in on the party where they stand; the world stays live around the fight. The battle camera MUST hold the same 55-degree pitch as exploration so the world lane keeps its single-pitch guarantee — only zoom and lateral swing may change.

IN — The one licensed exception to the fixed pitch is a combo finisher: a scripted 2-3 second cut may break pitch, framing and time scale, because it reads as deliberate flourish. It must return to the locked pitch when it ends.

IN — Because battle inherits whatever terrain, clutter, weather and time of day the encounter fired in, stage.mjs must verify the battle camera finds a clear framing in the WORST case, not the average: sample encounters in dense foliage, against a cliff, on a slope, and at night, and assert no actor is occluded and no combo finisher frames a rock instead of its caster.

IN — The world is a graph of twelve discrete maps ported from the prototype MAPS table, not one contiguous landmass: eight outdoor regions (haventide T1, emberline T2, forest_veil T2, mire_bog T2, orbital_reach T3, frost_canyon T3, crater_ember T4, last_crown T4) plus four city interiors. Each map is 45x30 tiles and self-contained. Emberline is the hub with four doorways; Haventide is the start.

IN — Every region carries its own tier (1-4), its own biome from the eight named biomes (grassland_ruins, neon_wastes, forest_veil, mire_bog, frozen_ruins, frost_canyon, crater_ember, alien_terraform), its own fixed encounter placements naming a specific enemy per spawn point, and its own doorway list. All 36 encounter placements and every doorway with its landing coordinates port forward unchanged. Enemies are placed, not randomly pooled.

IN — worldDrop is a SECOND loot source distinct from enemy drop tables: exactly one hidden item at a fixed tile per outdoor region, eight in total (bog_fang, glacial_claw, ember_core, void_scepter, moss_ward, swamp_coil, magma_blade, frost_plate). It must be findable by exploration and must survive a save/load round trip.

IN — Settlement build slots are per-city and live in the level data as the city plots array: inner and outer rings of slot positions in world coordinates around the town center landmark. The Tier 6 settlement grid reads those plots rather than inventing its own layout.

IN — The Map tab is a region-graph view, not a single scrollable plane: a thumbnail per region with its tier badge, the connecting edges, and live markers for active enemies, cleared regions, cities and world drops, with fast travel to any unlocked city. The prototype legend and keyboard model port forward.

IN — region.mjs walks the world graph offline and asserts it holds: every doorway target names a real map, every landing coordinate is inside that map bounds and passable, every edge is bidirectional unless deliberately one-way, every region is reachable from Haventide, every encounter names an enemy that exists in the tables, and every worldDrop names a real item. A typo in a mapId strands a region and no screenshot will ever show it.

IN — Region fidelity ships in two stages, but region CORRECTNESS never does. Tier 1 brings exactly two regions to full fidelity: Haventide (grassland_ruins, the T1 start) and Emberline (neon_wastes, the T2 hub) — deliberately two different biomes, so the system is proven to generalise rather than hand-tuned once. The other six regions ship BLOCKED IN from Tier 1 onward: correct footprint, elevation, collision, doorways, encounter placements and biome base palette, lit by the shared system, but with no bespoke vistas, no per-region set dressing and no authored landmark composition. Walkable and correct, not yet photogenic.

IN — Deferring fidelity never defers correctness. region.mjs, walk.mjs and door.mjs must pass on ALL twelve maps from Tier 1 onward, not just the two finished ones. A blocked-in region that is unreachable, untraversable or disconnected is a defect at the phase it appears in, not something the later buildout pass is allowed to inherit.

IN — A dedicated Region Buildout phase brings the remaining six regions (Forest Veil, Mire Bog, Orbital Reach, Frost Canyon, Crater Ember, Last Crown) to full fidelity as one repeatable pass, after the complete gameplay loop is proven in the first two. The critic scores each region individually; a region is not done because its neighbour passed.

IN — A Character Look Gate runs as early as physically possible, immediately after the design specs and BEFORE the harness and before any world work. It proves the code-built-rig approach on all THREE heroes at once — Kaida (armoured melee), Vex (robed caster), Rune (bulky tank) — because three deliberately different silhouettes is what proves a rig SYSTEM rather than one hand-tuned character. Nothing may be built on top of the rig approach until it has passed.

IN — The Character Look Gate must answer six questions with images, not opinions: does a low-poly rig plus pixel-snap plus palette-quantise read as a crisp pixel sprite rather than a muddy 3D model; does it hold at the locked 55-degree pitch specifically; does the silhouette read at 100px; do weapon swaps at hand sockets look right; does the SAME hero read as the same character across idle, run, cast, hurt, attack and victory; and does it survive three times of day in both Tier 1 biomes.

IN — rig.mjs proves character consistency as a NUMBER, not a judgement. It renders one rig across every pose and asserts the invariants a 3D rig gets for free and a generated sprite never could: identical palette histogram across poses (same geometry and materials must yield the same colours), silhouette area inside band, and no material drift in a fixed head and torso sample between poses. This is the exact defect that stalled the prototype art — a hero who looked slightly different in every stance — so it is measured from the first day rather than eyeballed.

IN — The pivot budget on the character approach is TWO rounds, and it is a hard stop. If the Character Look Gate fails twice, work halts and the approach is reconsidered from scratch with the user rather than iterated a third time. The prototype burned four pivots on character art with no gate to stop it; this constraint exists specifically to make the fourth pivot impossible.

IN — No spec ships from Foundations without the smallest executable artifact that could prove it wrong. A design document nobody has run is a hypothesis, and four such documents handed to four lanes is how a project discovers in Phase 7 that its Phase 1 was fiction. The artifact must be the SMALLEST thing that can fail, not a head start on the feature — an agent that builds the battle system in Foundations has broken the phase, not exceeded it.

IN — gamedesign proves the ENCOUNTER TRANSITION in Foundations, with primitives and no rig: three capsules for the party, capsules for enemies, a ground plane and representative clutter. It must answer whether the lateral swing and push-in at locked 55-degree pitch finds a clean framing in the WORST cases — dense foliage, against a cliff, on a slope, at night — with no actor occluded, and how long the transition takes before it reads as a stutter rather than a move. This is the newest and least validated decision in the project and the one that is most expensive to reverse late.

IN — level proves the world graph in Foundations by emitting the twelve maps as real data files and validating them offline: every doorway target resolves to a real map, every landing coordinate is in-bounds and passable, every encounter names an enemy that exists in the tables, every worldDrop names a real item, and every region is reachable from Haventide. This is the embryo of region.mjs.

IN — audio proves synthesis in Foundations by actually synthesising four signature sounds to audio files a human can play — combo stinger, resource tick chime, footfall, and hit crunch — rather than describing them. A written audio spec cannot reveal that code-synthesised SFX sound like beeps.

IN — The Encounter Framing POC must emit a combat clearance number: the minimum clear space an encounter needs around it for the push-in to frame every actor. That number is a hard input to encounter placement, which is why the POC runs in Foundations while level is still authoring rather than after 36 encounters are placed.

IN — ATB correctness is NOT an early gate. The math is a port of already-tuned prototype numbers: low risk of being wrong and cheap to correct, with nothing structural built on top of it. duel.mjs validates it at Tier 4, which is the right place. Early gates are reserved for decisions that are unvalidated AND expensive to reverse.

IN — Every builder phase runs in three waves, never as one crowd: (1) builder lanes in parallel, each isolated to its own folder; (2) the integrator ALONE, applying core seams and proving every previously green probe still exits zero; (3) the critic ALONE, taking its own shots and scoring. A critic must never be spawned alongside the builder it is grading — it would review a moving target and its score would mean nothing. A phase listing seven agents describes who participates, not who runs simultaneously.

IN — Phases are split into numbered sub-phases only where the ordering is specific to that phase and would otherwise be invisible. The uniform builder-integrator-critic wave pattern is a standing rule rather than repeated sub-phases, because a plan that states the same three steps seven times buries the one place the order is actually unusual.

IN — Tier 1 must land a resolved depth and normal prepass in the render path, even if no effect consumes it yet. Ambient occlusion, contact shadows and depth of field are all fit-and-finish effects that can drop in at any later phase — but only if the buffer they read exists. Depth cannot share the MSAA scene target, so retrofitting the prepass into a finished render path is structural work, while adding the effects on top of an existing prepass is not. Build the plumbing early and the polish stays cheap.

team.notes: Owns the engine, the shared ctx, all six stack-ranked tiers, and tools/ — the 13-probe verification harness is dev's deliverable, not an afterthought. Never merged.
Runs every probe between waves and regression-sweeps six scenes (world, traversal, interiors, battle, menus, settlement) that must not break each other. Never merged.

Redefined for this game: owns the code-built 3D rig system, socket and pose library, the pixel-snap plus palette-quantise shader that makes a rig read as a sprite, the palette, and the UI chrome rebuild. Owns no sprite production because the concept forbids binary assets. Carries the Character Look Gate — the earliest and hardest gate in the project, and the one the prototype never had.

Owns the twelve-map world graph ported from the prototype MAPS table: eight outdoor regions plus four city interiors, each with tier, biome, fixed encounter placements, doorway edges with landing coordinates, one worldDrop, and per-city build plots. Adds elevation and vertical interest to each region without changing its footprint, connectivity, or encounter placement. A massive standalone deliverable. Ships the twelve maps as validated data files in Foundations — the embryo of region.mjs. Encounter placement must respect the combat clearance number the Foundations POC emits.

Ports the prototype battle.js and progression.js math into an authoritative spec (ATB rates, enemy tiers, tech tables, drop tables, economy curves), then owns battle-camera choreography and economy re-verification via econ.mjs. Design is ported and verified here, not reinvented. Ships the Encounter Framing POC in Foundations — primitives only — to validate the fight-in-place push-in before anything is built on it, and to emit the combat clearance number encounter placement depends on. ATB correctness is deliberately NOT gated early; duel.mjs catches it at Tier 4.

Synthwave ambient beds per biome, combo stingers, resource-tick chimes and battle SFX — all synthesised in code via Web Audio, since the concept forbids binary assets including samples. Ships four synthesised signature sounds as playable files in Foundations, not a written description of them.
Localhost confirmation in Phase 0, then a GitHub Pages redeploy after each playable tier so the user can beta-test while later tiers continue. Absorbs release.
The only agent permitted to edit shared core. Runs between waves from Phase 3 onward, applying builders' core-seam requests and enforcing the CONTRACT.md ownership table across six parallel lanes.

Writes no code. Takes its own shots at several times of day and zoom levels, runs the lane probe, and scores 0-10 with the prototype as the 5 and the fixed defect list as the 8.5. Gates every visual tier.

Runs last. This is the first tech9 game to use code-built rigs instead of generated sprites and the first to ship the verification harness before the game — both lessons directly change the framework defaults for the next game.
Merged per asset.merge.candidates. There are no binary assets to produce — the concept forbids them outright — and rig construction is art direction work in this game.
Merged per release.merge.candidates. Static GitHub Pages deploy with no store page or marketing copy; versioning and changelog fold into devops.
Skipped. The game is not launched and no player-support or hotfix rotation is in scope for v1. Revisit only after public release.
Skipped. rendering_tier is threejs, and dev and godot_dev are never both active.

phases.name: Phase 0 — Engine Skeleton, Contract & First Light
phases.description: Vite + Three.js boot, the shared ctx object, the window.__DAWN__ debug API, ARCHITECTURE.md and CONTRACT.md with the binding file-ownership table, and the first two probes (shot.mjs, probe). DevOps confirms localhost serves and configures the GitHub Pages target without deploying yet.
phases.qa_gate: Localhost serves the page with zero console errors; tools/shot.mjs captures a PNG of a lit test scene and exits 0; ARCHITECTURE.md and CONTRACT.md exist and the ownership table covers every planned folder.

phases.name: Phase 1.1 — Foundations & Paper Prototypes
phases.description: Specs, each shipped with the smallest executable artifact that could prove it wrong. art specifies the code-built rig system (topology, sockets, pose library) and the pixel-snap plus palette-quantise approach — its proof is Phase 2. gamedesign ports the prototype math into an authoritative spec (validated later by duel.mjs, not here) AND builds the Encounter Framing POC: primitives only, no rig, proving the lateral swing and push-in at locked pitch finds a clean framing in dense foliage, against a cliff, on a slope and at night — and emitting the minimum combat clearance number that encounter placement must respect. level delivers the twelve-map graph with elevation and biome boundaries AS DATA FILES, validates them offline for connectivity, landing coordinates and content references, and authors provisional encounter placements — provisional because the clearance number does not exist yet. audio writes the synthesis catalog AND synthesises four signature sounds to playable audio files. Artifacts are the smallest thing that can fail — not a head start on the feature.
phases.qa_gate: Four specs exist and agree with each other; every one of the eight named prototype defects has a named owner; no spec requires a binary asset or a network fetch. The Encounter Framing POC shows a clean push-in framing with zero occluded actors in all four worst cases and reports a combat clearance number. The world graph validates offline with zero dangling doorways and every region reachable from Haventide. Four synthesised sounds exist as files and have been listened to. A spec whose artifact was not run does not pass this gate.

phases.name: Phase 1.2 — Encounter Placement Pass
phases.description: The one handoff inside Foundations that is invisible if left implicit. gamedesign has emitted a combat clearance number; level now validates all 36 provisional encounter placements against it and moves the ones that fail. An encounter sited with less than the required clear space around it cannot be framed by the push-in, and that is a level-data defect, not a battle-lane problem to solve later. Runs after 1.1 because the number cannot exist before the POC.
phases.qa_gate: Every one of the 36 encounter placements satisfies the combat clearance number, or is explicitly annotated as a deliberate tight-quarters fight that the battle lane must handle specially; the region data still validates offline with zero dangling doorways; the moved placements have not broken any doorway or worldDrop position.

phases.name: Phase 2 — Character Look Gate
phases.description: The riskiest unknown in the project, answered before anything can depend on it. art builds a working rig prototype for ALL THREE heroes — Kaida, Vex, Rune — plus the pixel-snap and palette-quantise pass and the socket system for swappable weapons. dev delivers rig.mjs. Renders each hero in six poses (idle, run, cast, hurt, attack, victory), each with three different weapons, at the locked 55-degree pitch, at three times of day, in both Tier 1 biomes. No world work, no traversal, no integration — a showcase scene and a scorecard. If this fails twice, work stops and the approach is reconsidered with the user rather than iterated again.
phases.qa_gate: rig.mjs reports identical palette histograms across all six poses per hero, silhouette area inside band, and zero material drift in the fixed head and torso sample; every hero reads as a crisp pixel silhouette at 100px and at locked pitch; the same hero is unmistakably the same character across all six poses and all three weapons; critic scores >=8.5 on the character look in both Tier 1 biomes at all three times of day. Two failed rounds is a hard stop, not a third attempt.

phases.name: Phase 3 — The Harness
phases.description: Build the remaining eleven tools (rig.mjs shipped with the Character Look Gate; region.mjs grows from the Foundations graph validation rather than starting cold): sheet, blind, walk, door, duel, stage, fog, econ, save, digest, census, region. Every module ships a showcase mode staging a representative scene of just that module.
phases.qa_gate: All 15 tools run against the skeleton and exit 0 or fail loudly with a real reason; census and digest are green; every probe prints numbers rather than a verdict alone.

phases.name: Phase 4 — Tier 1: World & Light
phases.description: Terrain with real elevation, the overhead camera rig at locked 55-degree pitch, sun/sky/IBL, time of day, weather that lands on surfaces, the post chain, and soft continuous fog of war. Haventide (grassland_ruins) and Emberline (neon_wastes) are brought to FULL fidelity — two different biomes, so the system is proven to generalise. The other six regions ship blocked in: correct footprint, elevation, collision, doorways and encounter placements, lit by the shared system, no bespoke set dressing. Fixes defects 1, 2, 5 and 6. First GitHub Pages deploy.
phases.qa_gate: A resolved depth and normal prepass exists in the render path and is verified by a probe, whether or not any effect consumes it yet; region.mjs reports a fully connected twelve-map graph with every region reachable from Haventide and zero dangling doorways — blocked-in regions included, no exemptions; fog.mjs reports a continuous field with no step discontinuity at any tile boundary; zero grid lines in any capture; free camera finds no unlit or untextured region in Haventide or Emberline; critic scores >=8.5 on BOTH finished regions with zero console errors; build is live.

phases.name: Phase 5 — Tier 2: Traversal
phases.description: Party of three moves — WASD and click-to-move, follower spacing, collision, footfalls matched to surface material, camera damping, locomotion poses on the rigs, and real contact shadows under every actor.
phases.qa_gate: walk.mjs exits 0 over a scripted three-minute route: 60fps sustained, zero collision escapes, zero clips through geometry, camera jitter inside budget, party arrives; critic >=8.5.

phases.name: Phase 6 — Tier 3: Places & Interiors
phases.description: Cities and buildings entered and left through real doors with their own interior lighting and a transition both ways. NPCs, shops and the forge.
phases.qa_gate: door.mjs walks every doorway in the twelve-map graph and exits 0, including region-to-region chrono-rift edges and all four city interiors — correct return position and facing, no soft-lock, load hitch inside budget; critic >=8.5 on interior lighting.

phases.name: Phase 7 — Tier 4: Encounters & Battle
phases.description: Roaming enemies, in-place battle start with a lateral swing and push-in at locked pitch (no scene swap, no load), ATB gauges, single-target and AoE techs, dual and triple techs, time-freeze crits, camera cuts on combo finishers, portrait flashes and elemental VFX. Fixes defects 3 and 4. Redeploy.
phases.qa_gate: duel.mjs resolves 200 seeded battles with zero deadlocks, time-to-kill inside band, and an observed loot distribution matching the declared drop tables with no item stuck at zero; stage.mjs confirms every combo finisher frames its own actors and the cut lands on the hit, AND that the push-in finds a clear framing in worst-case terrain (dense foliage, against a cliff, on a slope, at night) with no occluded actor; critic >=8.5; build is live.

phases.name: Phase 8 — Tier 5: Progression & Menus
phases.description: XP, levels, an owned-item grid with three gear slots per hero, equippable by click-then-slot and by drag-and-drop, skill trees, and the seven-tab pause overlay ported from the prototype verbatim in structure and keyboard model, re-skinned per defect 7. Quest log and localStorage save.
phases.qa_gate: save.mjs round-trips the full game state byte-identical; every equip shows a correct stat-diff preview BEFORE committing, via both click-then-slot and drag-and-drop; census.mjs reports zero orphaned items and all eight worldDrops are placed, findable and survive save/load; all seven tabs navigate by Q/E and 1-7; critic >=8.5 on menu chrome and HUD.

phases.name: Phase 9 — Tier 6: Settlement & Economy
phases.description: Settlement reads the per-city plots rings from level data. Town center, farms, mines, energy extractors, workers, resource ticks, and four tech tiers that visibly transform the base.
phases.qa_gate: econ.mjs simulates four hours of game time with no starvation and no runaway on any resource curve; a tier-up is unmistakable in a single screenshot.

phases.name: Phase 10 — Region Buildout
phases.description: Bring the remaining six regions to full fidelity as one repeatable pass, now that the complete loop — traverse, enter, fight, level, build — is proven in Haventide and Emberline. Forest Veil (forest_veil), Mire Bog (mire_bog), Orbital Reach (frozen_ruins), Frost Canyon (frost_canyon), Crater Ember (crater_ember), Last Crown (alien_terraform). Each gets its bespoke vistas, set dressing and landmark composition; each keeps its existing footprint, doorways and encounter placements unchanged.
phases.qa_gate: critic scores each of the six regions INDIVIDUALLY at >=8.5 — a region is not done because its neighbour passed; all eight biomes visually distinct in a contact sheet; region.mjs, walk.mjs and door.mjs still green across all twelve maps; frame budget held in the densest region; build is live.

phases.name: Phase 11 — Vertical Slice, Blind Gate & Release
phases.description: The slice: dawn over the coast, into a city, into a shop, out to an encounter, win the fight, spend the loot. Whole-game critic pass, then blind A/B judging against the prototype at matched location, time and framing. v1.0.0 tag, changelog, final deploy. Historian writes the lessons.
phases.qa_gate: Blind judges prefer Dawn at matched framing and can tell which is the remake; full slice playable with zero console errors; every probe green; v1.0.0 live on GitHub Pages; lessons written to meta/LESSONS.md.

deferred_decisions.decision: Rig topology, joint count, pose library size, and the pixel-snap/palette-quantise shader parameters that make a 3D rig read as pixel art

Orthographic scale at the locked 55-degree pitch, depth-of-field falloff curve, camera damping constants, and the full post-processing chain order and parameters (the pitch itself and the no-rotation/no-zoom model are decided, not deferred)
World map layout, elevation profile, biome boundaries, city and door placement, encounter density, and the difficulty curve
Battle camera choreography — cut timings, framing rules per tech, and the time-freeze and screen-shake envelopes
Fog-of-war field representation and the continuity threshold the fog probe asserts against
Synthwave ambient beds, combo stingers, resource-tick chimes and battle SFX, all synthesised in code

Shop and forge currency — the prototype has no trade currency (its cost fields are skill and building costs), so decide whether shops trade in renown, a new salvage currency, or barter against the settlement resource pool
